newsitem.title: USA: Job layoffs at lowest level in four years, survey says.
newsitem.headline: Job layoffs at lowest level in four years, survey says.

text.p: Happy days are here again for American workers.

Corporate America held on to its employees in April, as jobs-cuts fell nearly 70 percent from a month earlier to the lowest levels in four years, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc. said Wednesday.
A total of 15,214 job cuts were announced in April, it said, a drop of 69.7 percent from March, when 50,182 jobs were cut.
The April job-cut level also represented a 50.6 percent drop from April of last year, when 30,810 jobs were lost.
Challenger said the jobs market is improving for many workers as the labor market tightens.

"The fact that job cuts dropped so dramatically while at the same time hiring was lower than expected in April is evidence that the country is at virtually full employment," said John Challenger, executive vice president.
"In a situation like this employees are likely working more overtime hours and doing jobs of two or more people," he said.
"Employers must now assign more tasks than in the past since they cannot hire additional staff because of the labor shortage," said Challenger.
Indeed, U.S. workers stand a better chance of finding work as the economy continues to grow and the unemployment rate is the lowest in nearly a quarter century.
Last Friday, the Labor Department reported that the jobless rate fell to 4.9 percent in April from 5.2 percent in March. The 4.9 percent jobless rate matched a level last seen in December 1973.

The jobs report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in April, came on the heels of a report that the economy grew at a nine-year-high annual rate of 5.6 percent in the first quarter.

The outplacement firm said that in April, consumer goods companies led the list of job-cuts, with 3,086. This was followed by computer companies, which cut 2,528 jobs. Makers of industrial goods trimmed 1,579, aerospace-defense companies lost 1,499 positions and utility companies announced 1,038 job cuts.
According to Challenger, more individuals are getting full-time jobs with established companies.
It said that a major pool of potential employees is the record 1.2 million college students that are set to graduate this Spring.

"The tight labor market will benefit a large portion of these graduates," Challenger said. "However, many companies are seeking experienced workers who need little to no training and can jump right in and begin contributing."
He said the changing labor market also may benefit older workers.
"More and more companies are going to have to look at the other end of the age spectrum," Challenger said. "The over-50 worker has much to offer an employer."
